item.title: The Upside of Mental Flexibility
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

The Upside of Mental Flexibility

The agile pivots in any situation—it is tongbian 通變, we pass through and change.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • A rigid person can experience heated emotional reactions that lead to feeling overwhelmed and paralyzed.
  • To build more flexibility, we can also use present-moment awareness to manage our thoughts and emotions.

Stewart Butterfield spent years developing a massive multiplayer online game that failed to attract enough players; it was a financial bust. During the game's development, however, he and his team built a custom chat tool to coordinate remote work, one that was more successful than the game itself. This chat tool was repurposed into the messaging platform Slack, which Salesforce acquired in 2021 for $27.7 billion.

One can argue that this type of pivot is a good example of flexible thinking, the complete opposite of rigidity. A rigid person can experience heated emotional reactions that lead to feeling overwhelmed and paralyzed. Essentially, strong emotions restrict the brain from problem-solving; however, a flexible thinker can brainstorm solutions. An adaptable person can pivot in any situation—it is tongbian 通變, to pass through and change.

Source: AI Generated

The idea of go-with-the-flow unflappability can be found in many areas of therapeutic inquiry, including Gestalt, cognitive behavioral therapy, and acceptance and commitment therapy. Psychologist Steven Hayes, a professor of psychology at the University of Nevada and originator of acceptance and commitment therapy, has closely examined this ability. (Hayes may be a bit Buddhist.)

Hayes and his colleagues derived the “Acceptance and Action Questionnaire,” which measures just how mentally rigid a person can be, and they determined that a rigid person has the following negative tendencies:

  • Ruminates more and can get stuck in pessimistic loops.

  • Feels more anxious.

  • Feels more depressed.

  • Fears failure and success.

  • Seeks perfection.

  • Seeks approval from others.

  • Suffers more mental health conditions, including mood disorders and beyond.

  • Suffers an inability to learn, be curious, or open and relies on habitual responses.

  • Cannot expand or grow with new experiences.

  • Falls into self-sabotaging behaviors such as substance abuse, eating disorders, and procrastination.

By contrast, an emotionally agile and flexible person adapts to whatever a situation might call for. He balances different needs in different domains of life by making conscious choices about the time and energy spent on work, home, health, and other areas. He reshapes his mental resources and accesses different perspectives by observing his thoughts and feelings without getting entangled in unhelpful thinking patterns. This person is light on his feet and is adaptive rather than maladaptive because he realizes thoughts and feelings are not an accurate reflection of reality, which allows a more flexible view of life situations. He is resilient and doesn’t buckle in the face of adversity by engaging in self-compassion, which builds inner strength. He is broad-minded and does not rely on one tool or method to get through life, but tests different strategies and gathers information on what works or what doesn’t.

To build more flexibility, we can also use present-moment awareness to manage our thoughts and emotions. Doing so may help us attain what we want in life—the things we value and are dear to us. When we get mired inside our heads about slights, annoyances, grievances, fears, criticisms, insults, or whatever gloom we glom onto, we are not paying attention to what matters. We forget what is meaningful.

Here’s an example of what this means. Your child asks you why the sky is blue. You want to be the best parent you can be, but you’re not fully engaged with him because you’re thinking about a criticism leveled at you during the workday. In this half-state, you’re not likely to address your work life in a useful manner, nor will you be the parent you want to be. In effect, you’re not getting much done or remembering what is meaningful.

A mentally flexible individual can regulate his emotions and adjust them to whatever his surroundings demand. In research conducted by George Bonanno, a professor of psychology at Columbia University and the author of The Other Side of Sadness, people who can modulate their facial expressions while looking at emotion-filled images have better mental health than those who could not.

Showing our emotions is part of everyday social interaction. When a friend tells us she met someone special, we should show her our interest and enthusiasm. According to Bonanno and his colleague Charles Burton, a research scientist at Yale University, we must sometimes show more or less emotion than we feel.

Bonanno and Burton developed the Flexible Regulation of Emotional Expression Scale in 2016; this scale measures expressive flexibility. Types of items on the scale include:

  • You receive a gift from a family member, but it’s a shirt you dislike. You have to show happy enthusiasm.

  • You’re attending the funeral of someone you don’t know. You have to be somber.

  • You’re a guest at a solemn religious ceremony, and the person sitting next to you just whispered a funny joke. You have to stifle your laughter.

Researchers, including Bonanno and Burton, show that people who regulate their emotions can quickly analyze new information because they can pull back and think rationally. This ability enables a person to see open possibilities before them and flexibly adapt to new situations. It also helps a person to set aside their knee-jerk reactions and solve problems that come up. People who can regulate how they feel generally have better relationships, romantic, professional, and otherwise.

item.title: Arranged vs. Free-Choice Marriages: Which Are Most Loving?
item.description:
Relationships

Arranged vs. Free-Choice Marriages: Which Are Most Loving?

Most Westerners say arranged marriages are loveless. A recent study disagrees.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Throughout history, many, if not most marriages were arranged by the spouses' parents,
  • In the West, that began to change around 1600, but many cultures continue to arrange marriages.
  • Are arranged marriages loving? Many Americans might express doubts.
  • But a recent study of five cultures shows that arranged marriages are often quite loving.

Throughout history, across hundreds of cultures worldwide, male-female marriage has been almost ubiquitous. From ancient times until the 17th century, almost all marriages were arranged by the future spouses’ families. Love between bride and groom was largely irrelevant. What mattered most was how marriages impacted the two families’ alliances and finances.

In Western Europe, arranged marriages were the norm until around 1600, when free-choice marriages—also known as love marriages—began becoming popular, eventually replacing the arranged variety. In Shakespeare’s The Taming of the Shrew, written in 1591, Baptista Mirola looks to arrange marriages for his two daughters, Katherine and Bianca. Katherine’s is arranged, and Baptista is auditioning men to find a spouse for Bianca. But she rebels, and elopes with a suitor she freely chooses. In Shakespeare’s other plays, marriages are often arranged, but there are plenty of free-choice love unions: Romeo and Juliet, Antony and Cleopatra, and Othello and Desdemona to name a few.

Western European colonization of what became the United States began after 1600, just as arranged marriage began yielding to love marriage. In the U.S., love marriage has long been the norm. But throughout American history, various ethnic groups have arranged marriages for their children. The practice persists to the present day among many Indian-Americans, Arab-Americans, ultra-orthodox Jews, and other ethnic groups.

Which raises a question: Are arranged marriages loving or loveless? Recently, an international team of researchers explored the dynamics of arranged marriages in five non-Western societies—and came up with findings that may surprise many Americans.

The Study

The researchers from Poland, Bolivia, India, Nigeria, and Russia interviewed 598 spouses—260 women, 238 men—living in five non-Western societies that practice both arranged and free-choice marriage: the Igbo of Nigeria (34 million people), the Meru of Tanzania (2 million), the Kimaru of Kenya (1.3 million), the Bhotiya of the Tibetan Himalayas (120,000), and the Tsimane of Bolivia (8,000). Studying cultures that practice both types a marriage meant that those interviewed had thought about both models.

The researchers obtained permission from each group’s leaders to conduct interviews. Then teams of researchers visited the groups’ villages. Each team included at least one local person who spoke the group’s language and understood its culture. All those interviewed were compensated with either $10 U.S. or gifts such as fish hooks or flour.

The researchers defined “love” as consisting of three components: intimacy, passion, and commitment. They characterized intimacy as trust, self-revelation, and friendship; passion as intense feelings of desire; and commitment as clear, conscious decisions to maintain the relationship throughout life.

The researchers asked those interviewed about their type of marriage, how long they’d been together, and how they felt their marriages embodied the three components of love: intimacy, passion, and commitment.

Roughly Half and Half

The interviewers asked dozens of questions designed to develop a nuanced picture of the participants’ feelings about their type of marriage—both pro and con. The replies were coded into 42 categories. In slightly more than half the categories (23), participants favored free-choice marriage, while in slightly less than half (19), they favored arranged .

Preferences for one or the other were largely the result of the groups’ cultures. The Tibetan Bhotiyas clearly favored free-choice marriage. The Nigerian Igbos and Bolivian Tsimane just as clearly preferred arranged. The Kenyan Kimeru honored both, but tilted somewhat toward free choice, while the Tazmanian Meru leaned slightly toward arranged.

What about love? Findings were all over the map. In two groups, the Igbo and Kimeru, there were no significant differences in love based on their type of marriage. Among two others, the Bhotiya and Tsimane, spouses in free-choice marriages reported greater intimacy. But in one culture, the Meru, spouses in arranged marriages enjoyed greater intimacy and passion. And among the Bhotiya, free-choice partners reported more passion, while among the Tsimane, free-choice partners declared greater commitment.

Hot to Cold, Cold to Hot

Previous studies of arranged vs. free-choice marriages have produced this adage: “Love matches start hot then grow cold. Arranged matches start cold and then grow hot.” The idea is that over time, spouses’ feeling evolve. But in four of the five cultures, marriage duration had no impact on love, except among the Bhotiya, and for them, love differences emerged only after 10 years of marriage, with free-choice coming out slightly ahead.

The researchers concluded: “Although those in free-choice and arranged marriages might experience love differently, the differences are rather small. Our findings challenge the Western perception that arranged marriages lack love. Arranged marriages appear to be as rich in love as free-choice marriages.”

Western Bias?

I live in the San Francisco Bay Area, a region with large populations of Indian and Afghan immigrant families, some of whom arrange their children’s marriages. Local media have noticed. Their reports usually reflect the Western bias that arranged marriages are “loveless,” “empty,” and might “abuse” the young people ordered to wed spouses they hardly know.

This study reveals the Western prejudice against arranged marriage to be ill-informed. Arranged marriages are often intimate, passionate, committed, and loving.

item.title: Frauds, Con Men, Liars, and Shame
item.description:
Deception

Frauds, Con Men, Liars, and Shame

Are compulsive liars capable of shame?

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Compulsive liars are different from fraudsters and con men because their lying is out of control.
  • Compulsive liars accept their sense of guilt because they value the admiration elicited by their lies.
  • The urge to impress others can outweigh the fear of having lies exposed.

The story behind any expose of a compulsive liar involves human suffering and, until we understand more fully the psychology of compulsive lying, the story is likely to turn into tragedy.

Mixed Feelings About Admiration

The discovery that our admiration has been misplaced and manipulated can be exhausting. Admiration is usually a positive feeling, but it uses up energy. It stirs thoughts about possibilities for others and for ourselves. It reorganizes the mental map of our own challenges and achievements relative to others. We can genuinely enjoy our admiration of others while also feeling burdened by the task of managing our relative sense of worth.

So, alongside the puzzle as to how a compulsive liar can feel OK about lying to friends and colleagues is the frisson we may feel when their lies are exposed. This mean pleasure arises from anger at being duped. Being "taken in" by someone is disorienting. We feel vulnerable, even targeted for our trust. The anger arises from our increased awareness of vulnerability to being hoodwinked. Relishing their public exposure reassures us of shared standards and values.

The Fascination With an Exposed Liar

Someone who commands admiration for amazing feats of excellence—athletic, academic, or moral—and then turns out to have fabricated these achievements is also a focus for our fascination. This arises, partly, from the puzzle as to how someone can be content to live with a false face. How can you lie about what you’ve done and be comfortable with yourself? How can you enjoy others’ good opinion when you know it is based on lies? "They have no shame," we often conclude. But shame is exactly what they do have.

A compulsive liar is very different from the frauds and con men we now come into contact with every day—those who try to trick us into giving away money or the personal details that allow them to steal our money. They are very different from undercover policemen or spies or reporters who present a "legend" for specific purposes. Though many crime writers explore the difficulty some people living their legends have at distinguishing their own false persona from who they "really are," those living double lives for a shared purpose are generally not dependent on their legend to shore up their deep self. Some may feel some genuine attachment for others to whom they present a false self, and therefore feel bad about deceiving them, but they do not feel shame—the stripping down of the self. When frauds, con men, and undercover workers (spies, law enforcement, or reporters) are exposed, they simply move on.

The Lying Starts From Shame

A compulsive liar, on the other hand, does not so much aim to trick others as to cover the shame of their own lack of self by eliciting your admiration. Your admiration warms and enlivens the little bits and pieces of a self that seems, to them, to be deficient, empty, perhaps even ugly. Lying may be deeply uncomfortable for them, but it gives them, from this perspective, the best self they think they can get.

Because others’ admiration is crucial to their fragile and distorted sense of self, they need constant reassurance. So they keep telling lies to elicit further admiration. They hope to construct such a dense facade of self-flattering stories that the flow of admiration is constant. If they feel it ebbing through familiarity or inattention, they invent another story. The urge for that injection of admiration is so great that they are often careless. Outrageous claims of derring-do are unfiltered by reflection, logic, or plausibility.

We puzzle over their recklessness: Don’t they know they are very likely, eventually, to be found out? But their hunger for others’ admiration overpowers the fear of exposure. This does not mean compulsive liars do not experience guilt, but it is a moral discomfort they accommodate because lying is, in their view, the speediest and most reliable means of garnering admiration. This does not mean that being exposed as a liar has no impact on them. The opposite is true: Being stripped of people’s admiration leaves them with no sense of self—the ultimate experience of shame.

Shame is different from guilt arising from regret at failing to live up to our personal moral standards. Shame comes from our social mirror. It means "losing face" among others. As psychiatrist James Gilligan has shown, shame involves mortification, a term that stems from the Latin mors, or death, and facere, which means to make. Shame is the making of death for the social self.

'Mortification' as Social Death

Many people experience mortification at some point in their lives. Some people—those of a low "caste" or group or who are for other reasons ill treated or otherwise deprived of respect, care and acknowledgement—experience mortification on a daily basis with signals from others that say, "You are unworthy" or "You don’t matter." Many survive experiences of mortification because they find other social circles in which they are respected and cared for (and about), with people who acknowledge their value and legitimacy. Or they ground their sense of self through pleasure in their activities and interests.

A compulsive liar, however, has no self beyond that reflected by others’ admiration. That is why their lies are out of control. They don’t mind that their social mirror presents a false image; their constant quest is for more and more admiration, regardless of the terms on which it is acquired. Of course, this leaves them extremely vulnerable when their lies are exposed. Without the trappings that clamor for others’ approval, stuck in the spotlight of public opprobrium, they have no self, a condition tantamount to death.

item.title: Resilience and Aging: A Reflection From the Camino
item.description:
Aging

Resilience and Aging: A Reflection From the Camino

Personal Perspective: Living well with aging and walking the Camino de Santiago.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Growth does not stop with age. Neuroscience tells us that the brain continues to change throughout our lives.
  • Aging can bring limitations, but we can build new capacities.
  • Resilience is not about doing what someone else can, but about discovering what remains possible for us.
The Camino de Santiago
Source: Elaine Miller-Karas 2026

The Camino de Santiago or “The Way,” is one of the world's oldest pilgrimages. For more than a thousand years, people from every walk of life have traveled across Europe to the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in northwestern Spain. Today, people walk the Camino to seek healing, grieve, celebrate, find clarity, challenge themselves physically, or reconnect with what matters most. Whatever brings us to the Camino, it has a remarkable way of becoming the journey we need.

The Fall, and the Helpers

The Camino began teaching me one of its most important lessons on my very first day: I fell.

It was not a graceful stumble. By the time I looked in the mirror, I resembled what I jokingly called a “prizefighter pilgrim,” covered with bruises and scrapes. As someone whose life's work has been devoted to helping others heal, I am usually the one offering assistance. Yet within moments of my fall, the Camino reminded me that those who spend their lives caring for others must also learn to receive care.

A man named Kenneth and his wife stopped to help me. A taxi driver named Angel appeared when I needed someone to carry me forward. A restaurant owner named Domingo offered warmth and nourishment when my body and spirit needed restoration. Then there was a nurse named Edison—whose name, meaning “the light,” felt especially fitting—who treated my injuries with such compassion that I felt cared for far beyond my physical wounds.

Looking back, I realize they were more than people I happened to meet. They became symbols of grace, appearing exactly when needed. They reminded me that resilience is not about never falling but about allowing ourselves to be held by others until we are ready to walk again.

The Lesson

That first day changed the way I understood the entire pilgrimage. Rather than measuring success by how many kilometers I could complete, I began measuring the journey by moments of connection, gratitude, humility, and presence. The Camino invited me to surrender the illusion that I needed to be strong all the time. Vulnerability, I discovered, is not the opposite of resilience but one of its greatest teachers.

Walking with my son became another gift. There were stretches when we walked together and many when we walked apart, each finding our own rhythm. He was younger and faster; I needed to walk at my own pace. He often arrived two hours before I did and greeted me at our destination. There was something wonderfully symbolic about that. Loving someone does not require walking at the same pace. We can travel differently and still make the journey together.

Only two years earlier, I was not in the physical condition to imagine completing such a journey. I worked hard to prepare, and my family and friends were somewhat surprised by my determination. There were times when I doubted I could reach Santiago. Yet step by step, day after day, I moved closer to my destination. The Camino became living proof that aging is not simply about what we lose. It can also be about discovering capacities we never knew we possessed.

The Possibility of Curiosity with Aging

The nervous system continues to learn and adapt throughout life. Resilience is not a fixed trait we either have or lack; it is a dynamic process of responding, adapting, recovering, and growing through challenges. The Camino affirmed something I have taught for decades through the Community Resiliency Model: Resilience is not the absence of struggle. It is our capacity to return, reconnect, and move forward—even after we have fallen. It involves not only our individual strengths, but also the strengths of our families and communities.

We live in a culture that often associates growing older with becoming less capable, less adventurous, and increasingly fragile. Certainly, aging brings changes. Our bodies change. We may walk more slowly. Recovery can take longer. Loss becomes an increasingly familiar part of life. But this is not the whole story. Resilience does not mean pretending we are 34 when we are 74. It means becoming curious about what this seventy-four-year-old body, brain, heart, and spirit can still learn and do.

Research in lifespan psychology also challenges the assumption that psychological well-being inevitably declines with age. Many older adults maintain considerable emotional well-being and develop sophisticated ways of regulating emotions and responding to life's challenges. As we grow older and become more aware that our time is finite, many of us become increasingly selective about how we spend it and with whom. Meaningful relationships and experiences can take on greater importance.

We sometimes confuse resilience with fierce independence. But social connection and support are among the important resources that help us adapt to adversity. Resilience is knowing when to reach out a hand—and when to take the hand being offered.

A Gentle Lesson of Hope

I also do not want to turn my experience into another expectation placed upon older adults. Not every 74-year-old can—or should—walk 109 kilometers. Older adults live with vastly different health conditions, abilities, economic circumstances, caregiving responsibilities, losses, and opportunities. The lesson of my Camino is not, “If I can do it, everyone can.”

The lesson is gentler and, I believe, more hopeful: We should not decide what is possible for another person simply because we observe their aged face, a slower gait, or a disability. Instead, let us meet one another with curiosity and respect. Let us ask, “What is possible for you in the here and now?”

Let us ask, “What else is true?” A person may be living with limitation, loss, pain, or the realities of an aging body—and at the same time, there can be strength, purpose, curiosity, wisdom, connection, joy, and possibilities yet to be discovered.

I arrived in Santiago with sore muscles, tired feet, and a grateful heart. I also arrived with a deeper appreciation that healing is rarely a solitary journey. We all need companions like my son. We need moments of surrender, and we need our Kenneths, Angels, Domingos, and Edisons.

The Camino is a reminder of life itself. We begin with a destination in mind, but it is the people we meet, the unexpected detours, the moments of vulnerability, and the kindness we receive along the way that transform us.

item.title: When Social Media Becomes Another Weapon of Abuse
item.description:
Domestic Violence

When Social Media Becomes Another Weapon of Abuse

Tips for protecting your privacy and peace online after leaving an abusive relationship.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Social media can become another tool that abusive people use to cause further harm.
  • Abuse can continue online through harassment, monitoring, and smear campaigns after separation.
  • Blocking an abusive ex can protect your peace, even when it cannot guarantee digital privacy.

Laura had been separated from her ex-partner for several months when a friend sent her a screenshot: Her ex had posted about her on social media.

He didn't use Laura's name, but the details were unmistakable. He described their relationship as “toxic,” called Laura manipulative, and suggested that she had divorced him when he was struggling. Several mutual friends had commented, offering sympathy and agreeing with his version of events.

Laura stared at the screenshot, her heart pounding. They don't know what really happened, she screamed inside.

Her first instinct was to respond. She wanted to explain everything: the screaming, the threats, the infidelity on his part, and all the things she had tolerated before finally leaving. She immediately had the feeling that she was back in the relationship for a moment: defending herself, explaining herself, and waiting anxiously to see what he would do next.

Source: Tung Lam / Pixabay

How to Protect Yourself on Social Media After Leaving an Abusive Relationship

Unfortunately, leaving an abusive relationship does not always mean the abuse ends. Sometimes, when an abusive partner can no longer control you in person, they look for other ways to maintain access, provoke a reaction, monitor your life, or damage your reputation. Social media can make this easier.

Technology has given abusive partners more ways than ever to maintain contact, monitor survivors, and attempt to damage their reputations after a relationship ends. Text messages, emails, phone calls, social media, shared accounts, location services, and other digital tools can all become avenues for unwanted contact or harassment.

Eventually, even the devices you once used for ordinary parts of your life can begin to feel threatening. This is one reason digital abuse should not be dismissed as somehow less serious simply because it happens through a screen. The medium may be different, but the underlying goal can be the same: to maintain power, access, control, or fear.

An ex-partner may, for example, create new accounts after being blocked, monitor your posts through mutual friends, send unwanted messages, post about you publicly, or use information they learned during the relationship to embarrass, threaten, or intimidate you. They may also begin a smear campaign, presenting themselves as the victim and portraying you as the problem.

When someone has spent months or years controlling, manipulating, or hurting you, watching them publicly rewrite the story can feel unbearable. You may find yourself wanting to defend yourself against every accusation and tell everyone what really happened.

There are steps you can take to protect both your digital privacy and your peace.

1. Assume nothing online is completely private: Hopefully, you have already changed your passwords and logged out of your social media, email, financial, and other important accounts on shared or previously used devices. But remember: Even if you block someone and make your accounts private, you cannot completely control who sees what you post. It is worth remembering that anything you post could potentially make its way back to your former partner. A mutual friend may share something you posted, for instance—or someone could take a screenshot, like with Laura's case.

2. Be thoughtful about what you post—and when: You shouldn't have to stop living your life because someone is mistreating you. At the same time, if you are concerned about stalking or harassment, you may want to limit information that makes it easier for someone to track your whereabouts. Avoid posting your exact location in real time or sharing detailed information about where you will be and when.

You can still share the beautiful vacation photos; just consider posting them after you've left the hotel.

3. Be intentional about mutual friends: One of the more difficult realities after leaving an abusive relationship is that information can travel through people who are not intentionally participating in the abuse. You do not necessarily need to cut off every person you and your former partner have in common. Instead, think carefully about who has demonstrated that they can respect your boundaries and keep information confidential.

Consider telling the people you trust what you need before something like this happens. You might say something like: “I don't want my ex to know where I am or what I'm doing. Please don't share my posts, location, or personal information with them.”

4. Remember that blocking is about your peace, too: I generally recommend blocking an abusive former partner when it is safe and appropriate to do so. But blocking cannot guarantee that someone will never see your posts or find information about you.

However, what blocking can do in many cases is protect you from repeatedly encountering them. You don't have to see their profile appear in your feed. Blocking is about your sanity as much as it is about your safety.

You can also ask friends not to give you updates about them: “Please don't send me screenshots or tell me what my ex is posting. If there's something I genuinely need to know for my safety, please let me know. Otherwise, I'd rather not see or hear about it.”

5. Don't let their smear campaign pull you back in: Your former partner may say things about you that are untrue. They may tell mutual friends that you were the problem. And you may desperately want to correct the record, Like Laura who said, "I need people to know what really happened!"

Wanting to defend yourself is a completely natural response. But before responding publicly, ask yourself what that response is likely to accomplish. Will it protect you? Or will it give someone who has already harmed you another opportunity to pull you into an argument and retraumatize you?

If you need support for domestic abuse, contact the U.S. National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233

Excerpted, in part, from my book Invisible Bruises: How a Better Understanding of the Patterns of Domestic Violence Can Help Survivors Navigate the Legal System

item.title: When Your Mother’s Diagnosis Unlocks Your Own
item.description:
AuDHD

When Your Mother’s Diagnosis Unlocks Your Own

Jordan Davis spent decades wondering why. Then her mother was diagnosed.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • AuDHD in women is frequently missed because of academic success and masking.
  • A parent’s late diagnosis can unlock a child’s own, even in adulthood.
  • Meltdowns in autism are involuntary responses, not character flaws.
  • Alpha-gal syndrome creates hidden barriers to standard ADHD treatment.
Jordan and Finley. The dog who started everything.
Source: Jordan Davis / Used with permission.

The Game She Hated Without Knowing Why

You probably know the game: A sibling gets as close to your face as possible without technically touching, and says, with great satisfaction: “I’m not touching you.”

For most children, it’s annoying. For Jordan Davis, it was unbearable. She never understood why until she was an adult.

“I never knew why I hated it so much,” she tells me. “Now I know it’s because I don’t like being touched. I’m sensitive to that.”

Jordan is the founder of the Canine Stroke Foundation, an advocate for animal health, and someone who has spent most of her life being told she was difficult. She is also, as of recently, a person with a name for what she has been experiencing since childhood: AuDHD, the co-occurrence of autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

The diagnosis came unexpectedly. There was no crisis or collapse. It came from a face-to-face conversation with her mother.

The “Eureka” Moment

Jordan’s mother is a doctor and one of the most clinically informed people in her life. Yet when her mother was diagnosed as autistic in her 70s, it was the first time either of them began to understand Jordan.

“I immediately thought I needed to be assessed, because we are so similar,” Jordan says. “She talked about a lifetime of bad memories due to social misunderstandings. It all made sense to her finally. I needed that clarity as well.”

Autism has a strong hereditary component. A parent’s diagnosis frequently illuminates a child’s own experience, even when that child is already an adult. What makes Jordan’s story unusual is the direction. Usually, it is a child’s diagnosis that prompts a parent to recognize similar traits in themselves. For Jordan, it happened the other way around: Her mother’s diagnosis gave her a way to understand experiences she had spent decades struggling to explain.

“We often get accused of being mean or rude when that was never the intention,” Jordan says. “As I read more about autism, I recognized so many characteristics in myself.”

Her mother, a physician, had not considered the possibility when Jordan was young. The reason may sound familiar to people who have encountered the challenges of neurodivergent diagnosis: “I was verbal and a good student, so neurodivergency was never considered.”

Understanding Autistic Meltdowns Misinterpreted as Bad Behavior

Autistic meltdowns are not tantrums. They are involuntary responses to sensory or emotional overload, and Jordan spent years not knowing that was what was happening to her.

Bright lights. Loud noises. Being touched. Being misunderstood.

“After a while of it, I would ‘melt down.’ I always feel like the worst person in the world afterwards, so I try hard not to get to that point.”

The person experiencing meltdowns has no more control over it than someone has over a stress-induced migraine. But they look, from the outside, like bad behaviour. And they are treated as such.

“No one ever tried to explain or address what was happening,” Jordan says. “Punishment for that behavior won’t change the behavior. It's involuntary.”

Her advice to adults caring for children like her is simple: “Find the cause. Ask your child what they are feeling. Ask if sounds, lights, or physical sensations are making it worse. Once you understand triggers, it’s easier to avoid them.”

The Medication Problem Nobody Warned Her About

For Jordan, getting a diagnosis brought another set of difficulties.

Shortly after her AuDHD diagnosis, she developed alpha-gal syndrome: an allergy to mammalian products triggered by a tick bite. Alpha-gal syndrome affects hundreds of thousands of people globally, and its implications for medication access are poorly understood even within healthcare settings. Most pharmaceutical capsules contain mammalian-derived gelatin and many active ingredients are processed using mammalian byproducts. For people with alpha-gal syndrome, identifying mammalian-derived ingredients in medications can be complicated, and exposure can trigger a systemic allergic reaction.

Jordan found this out the hard way.

She was abruptly taken off duloxetine without a grace period to switch to an alpha-gal-safe alternative. The withdrawal was severe: “Brain zaps. The lack of energy was unbearable. I felt like I was dying.” Eventually, an allergist found a workaround: the pellets inside the capsule, taken without the gelatin shell, with famotidine to counteract remaining mammalian byproducts. Half a dose later, her symptoms resolved.

But the problem didn’t end there. “No doctor or pharmacist has been willing to call the manufacturer for me,” she says. “I was told medications were safe, and when I took them, I broke out into hives.”

She recently left an emergency room after discovering staff had not checked whether the medications they were about to inject contained mammalian products. “I asked if they checked. They said they did not. I left.” [Jordan’s experience is specific to her medical circumstances and should not be taken as advice to stop or change medication. Moreover, it is not a reason to avoid medication: it is a reason to ask better questions of the system providing it.]

What Clarity Feels Like

Jordan is now pursuing a graduate certificate in veterinary science. She plans a master’s degree after that. The difference, she says, is that she now knows how she learns, what she needs, and what she can ask for.

“I had a perfect GPA until the stress became too much for me to function,” she says of her earlier studies. Lectures were difficult because of auditory processing problems. Other students, lights and even the temperature could become overwhelming. Without a diagnosis, she didn’t have the accommodations that might have helped. Over time, those difficulties slowly accumulated until it broke something.

The diagnosis didn’t undo the difficulties she had experienced. But it helped her understand why some things had been so difficult.

“Learning about yourself can help you cope with the world in every way,” she says. “The battle is never over. You will continue to learn about yourself and how to keep yourself grounded your entire life.”

The insight she describes as most impactful is surprisingly simple: “Realizing I’m not actually a bad person.”

The meltdowns, the perceived rudeness, the years of guilt for things she could not control—a diagnosis did not undo any of those experiences, but it gave her a different way to understand them.
